nameStory: The "trembling" in this fungus's name comes from its distinctive jelly-like, gelatinous texture that literally trembles and jiggles when you touch it. The "crust" part describes how it forms thin, spreading layers across rotting wood surfaces, looking almost like nature painted a wobbly, orange-brown coating on dead branches.
description: Trembling Crust is a unique wood-decay fungus that looks more like orange jelly than a typical mushroom. Instead of having a cap and stem, it forms irregular, gelatinous patches that spread across the surface of rotting logs and branches. These rubbery, brain-like formations can range from bright orange to brownish-yellow and have a distinctly wrinkled, folded appearance. The patches can grow several inches across and have that characteristic trembling, bouncy texture when fresh.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Distinctly gelatinous and trembling - poke it gently and watch it jiggle like orange jello, feeling rubbery and bouncy to the touch

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright orange to orange-brown when fresh, fading to yellowish or pale brown as it dries out

idTips.label: Surface
idTips.description: Wrinkled and folded like a brain, with an irregular, bumpy surface that forms spreading crusts on wood

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows directly on rotting wood of both hardwoods and conifers, never on soil or other surfaces

idTips.label: Form
idTips.description: Forms irregular patches or crusts that can merge together, lacking any traditional mushroom cap or stem structure

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Usually has little to no distinctive odor, occasionally with a faint musty or woody scent

habitat: Look for Trembling Crust on rotting logs, fallen branches, and dead wood in New England's forests, from sea level to mountainous areas. It's equally at home in mixed hardwood forests, coniferous woods, and even urban parks where dead wood is present. You'll often find it alongside other wood-decay fungi on the same log, thriving in the moist, shaded conditions of forest floors.

seasonality.spring: Fresh, bright orange specimens begin appearing on wet wood as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture. This is when the jelly-like texture is most pronounced.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with the most vibrant specimens, especially after summer rainstorms. The gelatinous texture remains bouncy in humid conditions.
seasonality.fall: Still actively growing and easy to find, though colors may start fading to more yellowish tones. Specimens can persist through early frosts.
seasonality.winter: Dried specimens may persist on logs, appearing as shriveled, dark crusts that can rehydrate and regain their jelly-like texture during winter thaws.

funFact: This remarkable fungus can completely dry up into a hard, dark crust during dry spells, then magically spring back to life and regain its full jelly-like, trembling texture within hours of getting wet again - it's like nature's own sponge that never loses its bounce!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other orange jelly fungi like Witches' Butter, but Trembling Crust has that distinctive wrinkled, brain-like surface and always forms spreading crusts rather than blob-like masses. Remember: if it's trembling AND crusting across the wood surface with wrinkles, you've found the right one.
contextualKnowledge: You may see this fungus listed under its old scientific name Merulius tremellosus in older field guides, but it's now classified as Phlebia tremellosa. The name change reflects our better understanding of fungal relationships, but don't worry - it's the same orange, jiggly fungus either way!
compareHints: Unlike its relative Merulius croceus (which has a more papery, non-gelatinous texture), Trembling Crust maintains that distinctive jelly-like, bouncy quality. While both species decay wood, only Trembling Crust has that characteristic trembling texture and deeply wrinkled surface that looks like orange brain coral spread across rotting logs.
